walkthrough_label: STACKED CASE S1-C - true high potassium with ECG changes, acute kidney injury and a slow heart (heart-failure medicines)
reason_answer: To have my gallbladder taken out.

presentation.summary: Mrs Helena Novak, 71, is booked for keyhole gallbladder removal. She has heart failure and kidney disease, three days of diarrhoea last week, a slow pulse (52) and BP 104/62. Potassium 6.6, not haemolysed, with peaked T waves.

history.answer: I came for my gallbladder, but I feel dizzy when I stand and very tired.
Diarrhoea for three days last week, not eating or drinking much. Passing little urine today. No chest pain.
Heart failure with a weak pumping function. Chronic kidney disease (G3b).
Ramipril, spironolactone, bisoprolol and furosemide. I am still taking all my tablets despite not eating.
No anaesthetic problems in the family.

observations.note: HR 52 (scores 3 for 40 or less only; 41 to 50 scores 1, 51 to 90 scores 0); BP 104/62 (usual about 130/80).
After the emergency pathway is started by the clinician: rhythm improving.
Untreated hyperkalaemia: bradycardia, low BP, drowsy: risk of cardiac arrest.

examination.finding: Tired and dry-mouthed, alert, a little dizzy on standing.
Dry mucous membranes; low urine output.

results.comment: Severe hyperkalaemia (6.5 or more); not haemolysed
Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (baseline 112)

results.value: Tall peaked T waves with a slow rate
results.comment: ECG changes make this an emergency (picture result)

problems.label: Severe hyperkalaemia (6.6) with ECG changes
problems.why: UKKA: 6.5 or more is severe and any ECG change makes it an emergency; risk of fatal arrhythmia at induction.
expected_actions: Call the senior and the emergency team now
Treat without waiting for a repeat sample (ECG already abnormal)

problems.label: Acute kidney injury after diarrhoea (ramipril and spironolactone still taken)
problems.why: Reduces potassium excretion; the medicines are reviewed by the clinician.

problems.label: Slow heart and low BP
problems.why: Beta-blocker and hyperkalaemia both slow the heart; risk of collapse at induction.

problems.label: The planned operation is cancelled
problems.why: Not an elective patient any more.

options.text: Check pulse and BP again, request an urgent 12-lead ECG and potassium, and tell the senior
Record it and proceed to the anaesthetic room

decisions.prompt: Potassium 6.6, not haemolysed, with peaked T waves. What now?

options.text: Emergency: senior and emergency team now, cardiac monitor; do not wait for a repeat
options.consequence: UKKA: any ECG change is an emergency.

options.text: Ask for a repeat sample first
Cancel it; treat the potassium and the kidney injury first; re-list after recovery

correct: Slow pulse and low BP noticed
recovery: Call for help and start the pathway

recognised: Acute kidney injury after diarrhoea (ramipril and spironolactone still taken)
debrief.why_priority: UKKA: 6.5 or more is severe and any ECG change makes it an emergency; risk of fatal arrhythmia at induction.
debrief.related: The findings in this case point to the same cause
debrief.trigger_escalation: Any value outside its safe band or any breach of a safety rule
debrief.if_ignored: Harm from the missed problem or an unsafe operation
debrief.remember: Treat what the ECG shows; do not wait for a repeat.

asa.why: Heart failure with a weak pumping function and kidney disease: moderately reduced heart function is ASA 3 and severely reduced is ASA 4; the slow pulse and low blood pressure today lean to 4.
